1.1: Abyssinia (al-Habasha) was the Christian kingdom across the Red Sea, roughly today's Ethiopia and Eritrea. Years later some of the first Muslims found safety there with its king, the Najashi (Ibn Ishaq).
1.2: Barakah is her own name; Umm Ayman, "the mother of Ayman", is a name of honour taken from her son (Ibn Sa'd, vol. 8). That she came from Abyssinia is in Ibn Shihab's words in Sahih Muslim 1771.
1.4: "She was not free": Ibn Shihab (Sahih Muslim 1771) calls her the slave-girl of 'Abdullah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib. The Prophet ﷺ later freed her (chapter 6), and the Qur'an counts freeing a slave among the steep, good deeds (90:12-13).
1.5: That 'Abdullah died before his son was born is in Sahih Muslim 1771 ("after the death of his father"). In Ibn Sa'd the Prophet ﷺ later points out his father's grave in Madina, in the house where they stayed (chapter 3).
2.1: The Prophet ﷺ is never shown in this game, at any age, not even as a baby. Where he is present, the picture leaves him out and a soft breeze passes over it.
2.4: "'Abd Allah left behind Umm Ayman, five camels ... and a flock of sheep, which the Prophet inherited" (Ibn Sa'd, vol. 1, from al-Waqidi). "Nursed" in the sources means she looked after and carried him; he was breast-fed by his mother and by wet-nurses such as Halimah.
3.1: Ibn Sa'd (vol. 1): when he was six his mother took him to her relatives of Banu 'Adi ibn al-Najjar in Madina, "and with him was his nurse Umm Ayman. They were riding two camels". They stayed a month in the house of al-Nabighah.
3.3: The Prophet's ﷺ own memories of that month, in Ibn Sa'd (vol. 1): "I used to play with Unaysah, a hand-maid of the Ansar ... and I used to fly pigeons with the boys of my maternal uncles", and "I obtained proficiency in swimming in a pond of Bani 'Adi ibn al-Najjar."
4.1: Al-Abwa lies between Makkah and Madina; Ibn Ishaq says Amina died there when he was six, on the way back from her relatives (in Ibn Kathir's Sira). Al-Waqidi adds that Umm Ayman was with them.
4.2: The books go on to discuss the fate of the Prophet's parents in the next life. Scholars differ on it, and the game leaves it out.
4.3: "Then Umm Ayman brought him to Makkah on the two camels which were with them" (Ibn Sa'd, vol. 1, from al-Waqidi, whose reports are weak by the standards of hadith; the outline of the story is not disputed).
5.2: "O blessed one! do not neglect this son of mine" (Ibn Sa'd, vol. 1). "Blessed one" is her own name, Barakah.
5.4: He was eight. "Umm Ayman said: I saw the Apostle of Allah weeping that day behind the bier of 'Abd al-Muttalib" (Ibn Sa'd, vol. 1).
6.1: When she was freed: Ibn Sa'd (vol. 8) says when he married Khadijah; Ibn Shihab in Sahih Muslim 1771 says only that he freed her and married her to Zayd.
6.2: Her first husband was 'Ubayd ibn Zayd of the Khazraj. Their son Ayman became a Companion and was killed at Hunayn (Ibn Sa'd, vol. 8). Ibn 'Umar remembered how much the Prophet ﷺ loved the children of Umm Ayman (al-Bukhari 3737).
6.3: "O mother": Ibn Sa'd (vol. 8) records that he called her this. Years later a judge of Madina punished a man who tried to belittle her son by calling him "son of Barakah", saying the Prophet ﷺ had called her "O mother".
6.4: This saying is reported by Ibn Sa'd from Sufyan ibn 'Uqba, without a strong chain. Shia collections also count her among the people of Paradise (Muhsini, Mu'jam al-Ahadith al-Mu'tabara).
6.5:
Zayd ibn Haritha had been given to the Prophet ﷺ by Khadijah, and he freed him (Ibn Sa'd, vol. 8).

Umm Ayman married Zayd after her marriage to 'Ubayd ibn Zayd had ended. The sources read for this game (Ibn Sa'd, vol. 8; Ibn Shihab in Sahih Muslim 1771) do not say whether 'Ubayd died or they divorced; some retellings say he died, but give no early source. In Islam a woman is married to one husband at a time, so the game says only that her first marriage had ended.
7.1: The hijra to Madina was in 622. Ibn Sa'd (vol. 1) says Zayd brought Umm Ayman and Usamah; vol. 8 tells of her on the road at al-Munsarif, below al-Rawha'.
7.5: The bucket from the sky is reported by Ibn Sa'd from 'Uthman ibn al-Qasim. It is a story of a wonder (karama) without a strong chain, so the game says "it is told". She said: "No thirst afflicted me after that ... even when I fasted on a hot day."
8.1: "Umm Ayman was at Uhud and she was bringing water and treating the wounded, and she was at Khaybar" (Ibn Sa'd, vol. 8, from al-Waqidi). The game shows only her care, never the fighting.
9.1: Sahih Muslim 1771 and al-Bukhari 2630: Anas's mother had given the Prophet ﷺ date palms, and he gave them to Umm Ayman. After Khaybar the emigrants gave back what the Ansar had lent them, and he gave Umm Ayman trees from his own garden instead.
9.3: In Sahih Muslim 1771 Anas says she "put the cloth round my neck" and swore she would not give the trees back. The Prophet ﷺ kept offering more "until he had granted her ten times or nearly ten times more".
9.6: From Muhammad ibn Qays, in Ibn Sa'd (vol. 8): "The Messenger of Allah used to joke, but he only spoke the truth. All camels are the offspring of she-camels."
10.1: Umm Ayman's own account of Fatimah's wedding to 'Ali is in Ibn Sa'd (vol. 8): "I arranged her trousseau." Shia narrations (al-Saduq, al-Amali) also have her at the wedding, sad that nothing was scattered over the bride, and the Prophet ﷺ telling her of the gifts of Paradise at it.
10.4: You may hear (al-Saduq, al-Amali, from Imam al-Sadiq) that Umm Ayman dreamed "one of your limbs was lying in my house", that the Prophet ﷺ said it meant Fatimah would have al-Husayn, and that she carried the newborn to him. Sunni books tell the same dream of Umm al-Fadl, the wife of al-'Abbas (Ibn Majah 3923). The game leaves both out.
11.1: "Let us visit Umm Ayman as Allah's Messenger used to visit her" (Sahih Muslim 2454).
11.2: Sahih Muslim 2453: Anas did not know whether the Prophet ﷺ was fasting or simply did not want it, but "she raised her voice and showed annoyance to him". He loved her for her plain speaking.
11.3: When she died is not certain: five months after the Prophet ﷺ (Ibn Shihab, in Sahih Muslim 1771), or at the beginning of 'Uthman's caliphate (al-Waqidi, in Ibn Sa'd). The game does not say.
11.6: In Shia collections (al-Kafi; Tahdhib al-Ahkam) Umm Ayman is one of the witnesses Fatimah brought in the matter of Fadak, the land Fatimah held to be hers. Sunni and Shia accounts of Fadak differ, and the game does not tell it.
